name: Star anise (Illicium verum)
short: Infants given star anise tea (case reports): seizures, life-threatening event, liver failure (4-month-old, with green anise); Japanese star anise found in some. Outbreak, ages unstated: 16 seizures.
text: This entry covers star anise taken by mouth as a tea or infusion. Chinese star anise (Illicium verum) is used as a home remedy for infant colic; Japanese star anise, a neurotoxic plant named Illicium anisatum in most of the reports below and Illicium religiosum in one, can contaminate it or be blended with it, and the authors of one report say the two are hard to tell apart because the fruits are often sold broken or ground. Infants: a report describes adverse neurological reactions in 7 infants given star anise tea at home; the authors found evidence that Chinese star anise had been contaminated with Japanese star anise (the abstract does not say whether this was in these infants' tea) and conclude that star anise tea should no longer be given to infants. In a matched case-control study of infants under 3 months at two Madrid hospitals in 2001 (23 cases, mean age 29 days, with irritability, abnormal movements, vomiting and nystagmus), the symptoms were associated with anise infusion (Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio 18.0, interval 2.03 to 631), with odds ratios of 11.7 for low and 18.2 for high consumption, and laboratory analyses found Illicium verum contaminated by Illicium anisatum; the authors recommend that infants avoid anise infusions. Case reports in infants describe: convulsive status needing three doses of diazepam in a 1-month-old girl given a considerable amount of star anise for possible colic, with a favourable outcome; tremors or spasms, increased muscle tone, crying, nystagmus and vomiting in two infants under 6 months given star anise tea by their parents, with contamination proven in one; three episodes of central cyanosis and limb tetany in a 2-month-old given three bottles of star anise infusion for colic pains, with anisatin (the Japanese star anise toxin) in the infant's urine and 7800 micrograms per kg of anisatin in the fruit, against a Swiss maximum of 1000; abnormal movements, irritability and vomiting in a 2-week-old given star anise tea for colic; seizures, myoclonic jerks and irritability in a 4-week-old with colic fed a herbal mixture of star anise, who recovered quickly; toxicity in a 3-month-old; and liver failure with severe clotting problems, low blood sugar and seizures in a 4-month-old given a daily home-made star anise and green anise infusion for two months (the abstract does not separate the two plants or report contamination). Authors name both contamination with Japanese star anise and high doses of Chinese star anise as causes. Other reports (ages not given): in an outbreak investigated in 2001 by a national poisons control centre, 63 people of unstated ages had malaise, nausea and vomiting after a herbal tea that possibly contained Japanese star anise (anisatin was confirmed in the tea); 22 were admitted to hospital, 16 of them with generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and all were discharged in good health after supportive treatment. A case series from Bhutan describes two patients (ages not given) with gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms after eating star anise fruit, discharged after 24 hours of observation. Four more records known only by their titles describe an epileptic seizure after a cup of tea, attributed to intoxication with Japanese star anise, poisoning by star anise (Illicium verum) tea, and further cases of star anise poisoning; their titles give no ages and do not show whether any of these cases was part of the 2001 outbreak above. A 2010 letter, which has no abstract, is titled as raising safety concerns about star anise tea used to prevent swine flu. Allergy: a case report, known only by its title, describes anaphylaxis after treatment with the influenza medicine oseltamivir in a patient sensitised to star anise who had celery-carrot-mugwort-spice syndrome; the record has no abstract, so the link and the outcome cannot be reported. These are case reports, a case series and one case-control study; they cannot show how often harm occurs, and no trial reporting adverse events in people was found. No interaction data were found in the cited sources; the oseltamivir record above has no abstract and cannot show an interaction.
